taxonomy.note: Accepted by current Kew/POWO. Older Texas usage often misapplied Lantana horrida to this species; learner uses L. urticoides.

evidence: Kew/POWO accepts Lantana urticoides and lists Texas in the native range.
Travis County — UT Plant Resources Center's Travis County Verbenaceae herbarium index includes four L. urticoides specimens.
Williamson County — UT Plant Resources Center provides a full county treatment of naturally occurring L. urticoides.
Val Verde County — the Amistad National Recreation Area vascular flora documents L. urticoides on rocky slopes, flats, bluffs, and rock outcrops.
target_zone_range.guardrail: Texas lantana is heavily cultivated. Nursery/landscape plants and garden escapes are not used as native-county evidence.

morphology.look_here_first: Ignore flower color at first. Check the woody shrub habit, opposite rough leaves, and stems: Texas lantana is a winter-deciduous, non-spinescent shrub with stiff-hairy/scabrous 4-sided young stems and coarse serrate leaves. Then inspect the flower-head bracts and confirm the axillary pedunculate head.
diagnostic_traits: winter-deciduous aromatic shrub, commonly around 0.5–1 m in regional treatments
young stems four-sided, stiff-hairy/scabrous, aging woody
leaves opposite and decussate, broadly ovate to ovate, short-petiolate
leaf blades rough/cobblestone-textured above with stiff hairs and strongly raised veins below
dense axillary flower heads borne on distinct peduncles
flowers commonly open yellow and age through orange to red, but color is secondary to vegetative/bract characters

confusers.separator: A common non-native/invasive landscape escape. L. camara often has small prickles on the square stems and commonly larger leaves. Use inflorescence-bract structure and stem armature rather than flower color alone; absence of prickles by itself is not enough for a final ID.
Native desert lantana has much more slender branches, narrower hairy leaves, and typically white-to-pink flowers with yellow centers rather than the robust broad-leaved Texas-lantana look.
A common cultivated trailing lantana; habit is low/trailing rather than an upright woody Texas-lantana shrub, and flowers are usually lavender-purple.

diagnostic_roles: young four-sided stem showing absence of prickles
photo_verification.provenance_note: Prefer user's wild observations when they show stem armature, leaf texture, and head/bract structure. Public reuse remains photo-license dependent.
